claims.text: Low hardness and strength in simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi are controlled by intrinsically low lattice friction.
Low lattice friction permits rapid dislocation glide.
Facile dislocation glide promotes dynamic recovery.
The homogeneous single-phase state has only modest lattice distortion.
Dislocations nucleate and move easily in the homogeneous single-phase state.
Significant dislocation pile-ups and forest-hardening barriers do not accumulate in the starting state.
Limited barrier accumulation results in low work hardening, hardness, and yield strength.
Facile dislocation motion accounts for the high ductility of the alloy.
Facile dislocation motion accounts for the favorable machinability of the alloy.
The initial material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state without significant secondary phases.
The initial material has a relatively coarse to moderate grain size.
Severe plastic deformation can refine the grain structure and alter dislocation storage.
Low-temperature aging can induce nanoscale precipitates that impede dislocation glide.
Low lattice distortion and the absence of strengthening precipitates produce a low critical shear stress for dislocation glide.
Dynamic recovery occurs through dislocation annihilation at grain boundaries.
Dynamic recovery minimizes dislocation accumulation and work hardening.
The untreated alloy will exhibit relatively low hardness and yield strength together with high ductility.
Grain refinement or formation of fine coherent precipitates will measurably increase yield strength and hardness by increasing dislocation impediment and storage.
The strengthening produced by grain refinement or precipitation will reduce ductility.
The proposed mechanism applies under quasi-static loading from room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures and for micrometer-scale grain sizes.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts applicability to material processed without significant secondary-phase formation, but one principal intervention and prediction require deliberately forming nanoscale precipitates. The starting-state boundary is clear, but the applicability of the mechanism to the precipitate-containing comparison state is not.
